extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduate/graduate mathematics students and instructors (readers interested in nonstandard analysis and advanced problem-solving)
extracted.subtask_description: Working through advanced textbook exposition and appendix problems (including nonstandard analysis exposition, definitions, and a broad set of challenging exercises) intended to develop inventive mathematical ability rather than routine technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extension of number systems to secure desirable properties
rubrics_metrics.description: The extension from reals to hyperreals is just one further example of the ancient game of extending the number system in order to secure a desirable property. For example, the rational numbers were extended to the reals to allow √2 to exist; the reals were extended to the complex numbers to allow √-1 to exist; similarly we may extend R to R* to allow infinitesimals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use extension of number systems when a desirable algebraic or analytic property cannot be realized in the existing system; view hyperreals as an intended tool to realize infinitesimals in the same conceptual spirit as previous historic extensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of R* (hyperreals) to prove theorems about R via first-order transfer
rubrics_metrics.description: We can use R* to prove theorems about R, because the number systems R and R* are indistinguishable as far as first order properties are concerned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploit the transfer principle: first-order statements valid in R carry over to R*, and vice versa, enabling proofs about standard reals using hyperreal techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Key nonstandard definitions (finite, infinitesimal, infinite, nonstandard, standard part)
rubrics_metrics.description: A hyperreal number is finite if it is smaller than some standard real. It is infinitesimal if it is smaller than all positive standard reals. Anything not finite is infinite, and anything not in R is nonstandard. Every finite hyperreal x has a unique standard part std(x) which is infinitely close to x (x − std(x) is infinitesimal): each finite hyperreal has a unique expression as 'standard real plus infinitesimal.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt these definitions when working in R*; the notion of standard part (std) is central for connecting hyperreal statements back to standard real conclusions (the 'halo'/'shadow' imagery may aid intuition).

rubrics_metrics.name: Using the standard part to transfer properties and connect R* and R
rubrics_metrics.description: By using the standard part we can transfer properties from R* to R, or vice versa. Each finite hyperreal is 'standard real plus infinitesimal' and is surrounded by a halo of infinitely close hyperreals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In proofs, reduce statements about finite hyperreals to statements about their standard parts when wanting conclusions in R; the standard part operation is the main bridge between nonstandard and standard formulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonstandard definitions of continuity, derivative, and area
rubrics_metrics.description: Continuity at x: f(x+e) is infinitely close to f(x) (i.e., f(x+e) − f(x) is infinitesimal) for all infinitesimal e. Derivative at x: f has derivative d at x iff [f(x+Δx) − f(x)]/Δx is infinitely close to d for all infinitesimals Δx. Area of a curved region: an infinite sum of infinitesimal rectangles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use infinitesimal formulations as rigorous definitions within nonstandard analysis; these are exact analogues of epsilon-delta notions but often lead to shorter, more direct proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for choosing nonstandard analysis: simplicity and naturalness vs background cost
rubrics_metrics.description: Nonstandard analysis does not lead to different conclusions about R than standard analysis; the relevant question is whether it is a simpler or more natural way to derive those results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experience suggests nonstandard proofs are usually shorter and more direct because they avoid complicated size-estimate arguments (epsilon-delta); weigh this advantage against the obstacle that appreciating nonstandard analysis requires background emphasizing mathematical logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature of appendix problems: intended audience and pedagogical aim
rubrics_metrics.description: Many of the following problems are intended for the somewhat advanced reader. They are designed not so much to develop routine technique as to stimulate inventive ability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat starred or advanced exercises as challenges to develop creative problem-solving rather than mechanical practice; expect cross-references to text pages and invitations to devise multiple or novel solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration pedagogy: primitives and caution about 'indefinite integral' notation
rubrics_metrics.description: The theorem reduces the problem of integrating f(x) between limits a and b to finding a primitive G(x) for f(x); the integral is G(b) − G(a). The name 'indefinite integral' and notation G(x) = ∫ f(x) dx may be misleading for beginners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize the primitive (antiderivative) viewpoint when teaching/doing definite integration; warn beginners about potential confusion around indefinite integral notation and constants of integration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental integration rules: substitution and integration by parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Every formula of differentiation contains the solution of a problem of indefinite integration by interpreting it inversely. Two important rules in integral form are integration by substitution (from differentiation of a compound function) and integration by parts (from the product rule).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When solving indefinite integrals, look for an appropriate substitution derived from chain-rule structure or apply integration by parts when an integrand is a product; treat differentiation formulas as guides to integration formulas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification practice: check indefinite integral results by differentiation
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate the following indefinite integrals and verify the results by differentiation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After finding an antiderivative, always differentiate it to confirm it returns the original integrand (this is explicit instructional practice in the text).

rubrics_metrics.name: Derivation-specific guidance: substitution rule from x = p(u) and product-rule-derived integral identity
rubrics_metrics.description: The substitution rule results from the formula for the differentiation of a compound function x = p(u); the integration-by-parts identity follows from (p(x)·q(x))' = p(x)q'(x)+p'(x)q(x) and can be written in integral form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When deriving or applying these rules, follow the given derivations: express x as a function of a new variable for substitution; write product differentiation as an integral identity to obtain integration by parts formulas (the text gives the exact integral forms).
